# Argand lamp (hollow wick and glass chimney) (`argand_lamp`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by glassmaking, oxygen_combustion, petroleum_refining
- Core idea: An ordinary wick flame is starved of air in the middle, so it smokes and gives little light. Make the wick a hollow tube held between two metal tubes, so that air rises both inside and outside the ring of flame, and stand a glass chimney over it to strengthen the draught and steady the flame. The oil burns completely and one lamp gives the light of six to ten candles without smoke. A screw or rack raises the wick. Thick vegetable oil must stand above the burner or be pumped to it; thin lamp oil distilled from petroleum climbs the wick by itself.
- Pitfalls:
  - A hollow wick without the chimney, or a chimney without the central air passage; it needs both
  - A chimney of poor glass that cracks in the heat; early ones did
  - Volatile spirits (naphtha, strong alcohol mixtures) in a lamp made for oil: explosions and burns
- History: global: prehistory onward – open lamps with solid wicks burning fat or oil, in every culture; europe: 1780 – Ami Argand of Geneva builds the hollow-wick lamp (English patent 1784; made by Boulton, copied in Paris by Quinquet and Lange); 1800 Carcel's clockwork oil pump; 1853 Łukasiewicz's kerosene lamp at Lwów
- Read:
  - John J. Wolfe, Brandy, Balloons, & Lamps: Ami Argand, 1750–1803 (1999)
  - Wolfgang Schivelbusch, Disenchanted Night: The Industrialization of Light in the Nineteenth Century (1988)
